youtube.title_sentence: What Happens to an Ant Nest in Heavy Rain?
youtube.description_text:
Ants were building rain-proof cities long before us.

So why do a hundred thousand ants still end up floating? This Short shows what happens to an ant nest in heavy rain: first the defences built into the nest, then the backup plan when the water wins.

How an ant nest keeps the rain out:
• Wood ants thatch their mound with pine needles, layered like roof tiles, so rain runs off the dome.
• Some ants build a raised rim around the entrance, so water flows around the door, not in.
• Before a storm, some species seal their entrances with soil.
• Many chambers sit off to the side of the main tunnels, so water drains down past them into the soil.
• Workers carry the eggs up to the warm, dry top of the mound.

When the nest floods:
• Fire ants grab each other, jaws to legs, and weave a living raft.
• A whole colony links up in about a hundred seconds.
• Tiny hairs trap a layer of air, so the raft stays afloat.
• The queen and the young ride in the dry middle.
• The raft can drift for weeks until it reaches land.

Sources: Mlot, Tovey & Hu (2011), "Fire ants self-assemble into waterproof rafts to survive floods", PNAS 108(19); wood-ant (Formica) mound thatch studies; ant nest architecture (W. R. Tschinkel).
Animation, script and voice made by our studio. Rain sounds generated in-house.

instagram.title: Ants were building rain-proof cities long before us. 🐜🌧️
instagram.description:
So why do a hundred thousand ants still end up floating?

First, their defences: a pine-needle roof that sheds rain, a raised rim around the door, doors sealed with soil before a storm, tunnels that drain the water away, and eggs carried up to the warm, dry top of the mound.

But when the rain wins, fire ants grab each other, jaws to legs, and weave a living raft in about 100 seconds. Tiny hairs trap air so it can't sink. The queen rides in the dry middle, and the raft can drift for weeks until it finds land.
